overview.title: What Is IVF?
paragraphs: In vitro fertilization (IVF) is a form of assisted reproductive treatment. Eggs are collected from the ovaries and combined with sperm in a laboratory, where fertilization can take place outside the body.
The resulting embryos are monitored as they develop. An embryo may then be transferred to the uterus, with the aim of achieving a pregnancy.
overview.note: Your individual treatment plan may vary depending on your medical history and fertility assessment.

steps.caption: From the ovaries, in a planned procedure

steps.label: Embryo transfer

suitability.intro: A fertility specialist may discuss IVF in a number of different situations. These are some of the more common ones.

points.title: Tubal factors
points.text: When the fallopian tubes are blocked or damaged, which can prevent egg and sperm from meeting naturally.

points.title: Certain male-factor fertility concerns
points.text: Some sperm-related factors may make fertilization in the laboratory a helpful option.

points.title: Some cases of unexplained infertility
points.text: When investigations have not identified a clear cause and other approaches have been considered.

points.title: After previous fertility treatment
points.text: Where treatments such as ovulation induction or IUI have been tried, IVF may be considered as a next step.

points.title: Other fertility circumstances
points.text: Other situations in which assisted reproduction may be recommended after specialist evaluation.

suitability.note: IVF is not automatically the right treatment for everyone. Your fertility specialist can help determine whether it may be appropriate for your situation.

faqTitle: Questions You May Have About IVF

faqs.question: Is IVF suitable for everyone?
faqs.answer: No. IVF is one of several fertility treatment options. Whether it may be appropriate depends on a specialist's evaluation of your individual circumstances.

faqs.question: How does IVF differ from IUI?
faqs.answer: In IUI, prepared sperm is placed in the uterus around the time of ovulation and fertilization takes place inside the body. In IVF, eggs are collected and fertilized in a laboratory, and an embryo may then be transferred to the uterus.

faqs.question: What tests may be needed before IVF?
faqs.answer: This depends on your situation. Investigations may include blood tests, ultrasound scans and semen analysis, among others. Your doctor will recommend what is appropriate for you.

faqs.question: How long can IVF treatment take?
faqs.answer: The timeline varies with the treatment plan, medicines, monitoring and individual response. Your specialist will explain the expected timeline for your plan.

faqs.question: Is IVF painful?
faqs.answer: Experiences vary. Injections can cause brief discomfort, and some people feel bloating during stimulation. Egg retrieval is commonly carried out with sedation or anaesthesia. Your care team will explain what to expect and how discomfort is managed.

faqs.question: What happens during egg retrieval?
faqs.answer: Eggs are collected from the ovaries in a short procedure guided by ultrasound. Your team will explain how to prepare and how to rest afterwards.

faqs.question: What happens after embryo transfer?
faqs.answer: There is a waiting period before a pregnancy test. Your care team will tell you when to check in, any guidance to follow and the next steps.

faqs.question: How can I understand the cost of IVF?
faqs.answer: Costs depend on your treatment plan, medicines, investigations and any additional procedures. The clearest way to understand the cost for your situation is to speak with our team.

faqs.question: When should I speak with a fertility specialist?
faqs.answer: If you have concerns about conceiving, have been trying for some time without success, or have a known condition that may affect fertility, a consultation can help you understand your options.

faqs.question: Can I book a consultation before deciding on treatment?
faqs.answer: Yes. A consultation is an opportunity to discuss your concerns, understand your options and ask questions before making any decisions.

finalCta.title: Thinking About IVF?
finalCta.description: You don't need to have all the answers before your first consultation. Start with a conversation and understand your options.

overview.title: What Is IUI?
paragraphs: Intrauterine insemination (IUI) is a fertility treatment in which specially prepared sperm is placed directly into the uterus around the time of ovulation.
This brings sperm closer to the egg, and fertilization then takes place naturally inside the body. IUI may be done in a natural cycle or alongside medicines that support ovulation.
overview.note: Whether IUI is done in a natural or medicated cycle depends on your fertility assessment.

suitability.title: When Might IUI Be Considered?
suitability.intro: IUI is generally considered when at least one fallopian tube is open. A specialist may discuss it in situations such as:

points.title: Mild male-factor concerns
points.text: When sperm count or movement is slightly below the expected range.

points.title: Ovulation-related concerns
points.text: Often together with medicines that support ovulation.

points.title: Some cases of unexplained infertility
points.text: When investigations have not identified a clear cause.

points.title: Cervical factors
points.text: When cervical mucus may make it harder for sperm to reach the uterus.

points.title: Other fertility circumstances

suitability.note: IUI is not suitable for every situation — for example, when both fallopian tubes are blocked. Your specialist will help you understand whether it may be appropriate.

hero.title: Specialized Fertility Care, Tailored to Your Journey.
hero.description: ICSI is a specialized laboratory technique used as part of IVF, where a single sperm is injected into each mature egg. We help you understand when it may be recommended and what it involves.
hero.imageAlt: A laboratory specialist beside a microscope

overview.title: What Is ICSI?
paragraphs: Intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) is a laboratory technique performed during an IVF cycle. Instead of placing eggs and sperm together, an embryologist injects a single sperm directly into each mature egg.
ICSI aims to help fertilization when sperm may have difficulty reaching or entering the egg. The rest of the journey — stimulation, egg retrieval and embryo transfer — follows the IVF process.
overview.note: ICSI can assist fertilization, but it cannot guarantee that every egg will fertilize or develop.

steps.label: Eggs are collected
steps.caption: As part of an IVF cycle

suitability.title: When Might ICSI Be Considered?
suitability.intro: Your specialist and the embryology team may recommend ICSI in situations such as:

points.title: Male-factor fertility concerns
points.text: Such as low sperm count, reduced movement or differences in sperm shape.

points.title: Previous fertilization difficulties
points.text: When fertilization was limited in an earlier IVF cycle.

points.title: Surgically retrieved sperm
points.text: When sperm is collected through a procedure rather than a sample.

points.title: Limited frozen sperm
points.text: When only a small number of frozen sperm are available.

points.title: Other laboratory considerations
points.text: Situations identified by your specialist and embryology team.

suitability.note: ICSI is not needed for every IVF cycle. Whether it is recommended depends on your individual circumstances.

hero.description: Ovulation induction uses carefully monitored medicines to help the ovaries release an egg. Our team helps you understand whether it may suit your situation and supports you through each cycle.

overview.title: What Is Ovulation Induction?
paragraphs: Ovulation induction is a treatment that uses medicines to stimulate or regulate ovulation — the release of an egg from the ovary — in people who ovulate irregularly or not at all.
The cycle is usually monitored with scans, so ovulation can be timed. It may be followed by timed intercourse, or combined with IUI where appropriate.
overview.note: The medicines and approach used depend on your individual fertility assessment.

suitability.title: When Might Ovulation Induction Be Considered?
suitability.intro: A specialist may discuss ovulation induction in situations such as:

points.title: Irregular or absent ovulation
points.text: When cycles are irregular or ovulation is not happening regularly.

points.title: Some hormonal conditions
points.text: Including some people with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).

points.title: Some cases of unexplained infertility
points.text: Where supporting ovulation may be a reasonable step.

points.title: Alongside IUI
points.text: To support and time ovulation during an IUI cycle.

points.title: Other circumstances
points.text: Situations identified through specialist evaluation.

suitability.note: Ovulation induction is not the right approach for every fertility concern. Your specialist will help determine whether it may be appropriate for you.

faqTitle: Questions You May Have About Ovulation Induction

faqs.question: What is ovulation induction?
faqs.answer: It is a treatment that uses medicines to help the ovaries release an egg, usually with scans to monitor the response and time ovulation.

faqs.question: Is it tablets or injections?
faqs.answer: It can be either, depending on your situation. Your specialist will explain which medicine may suit you and why.

faqs.question: Why is monitoring important?
faqs.answer: Monitoring shows how the follicles are responding, helps time ovulation and allows your team to adjust the plan — including reducing the chance of releasing too many eggs.

faqs.question: Can ovulation induction be combined with IUI?
faqs.answer: Yes. Ovulation induction is sometimes used alongside IUI, where appropriate. Your specialist will discuss whether this may suit you.

faqs.question: Are there side effects?
faqs.answer: Some people notice side effects such as bloating, hot flushes or mood changes. Your team will explain what to look out for.

faqs.question: How many cycles might I need?
faqs.answer: This varies. Your specialist can discuss how many cycles may be reasonable and when other options might be considered.

faqs.question: Can I book a consultation before deciding?
faqs.answer: Yes. A consultation is a chance to understand your options and ask questions before deciding on treatment.

hero.title: Carefully Guided Embryo Development & Transfer.
hero.description: Blastocyst culture allows embryos to develop in the laboratory for a few more days before transfer. We help you understand how it fits into your IVF or ICSI journey.

overview.title: What Is Blastocyst Culture & Transfer?
paragraphs: During IVF or ICSI, embryos can be transferred after a few days, or kept in culture in the laboratory for longer. A blastocyst is an embryo that has developed for around five to six days after fertilization.
Culturing embryos to this stage gives the embryology team more time to observe development before an embryo is selected for transfer, or suitable embryos are frozen.
overview.note: Not every embryo reaches the blastocyst stage, and blastocyst culture is not recommended in every situation.

points.text: To see which embryos continue to develop before transfer.

faqTitle: Questions You May Have About Blastocyst Culture

faqs.question: What is a blastocyst?
faqs.answer: A blastocyst is an embryo that has developed for around five to six days after fertilization, reaching a more advanced stage of development.

faqs.question: Why culture embryos to the blastocyst stage?
faqs.answer: It gives the embryology team more time to observe development before an embryo is selected for transfer or freezing.

faqs.question: Will all my embryos reach the blastocyst stage?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. It is common for some embryos to stop developing earlier. Your team will keep you informed.

faqs.question: Is blastocyst culture always recommended?

faqs.question: Can blastocysts be frozen?

faqs.question: Can I book a consultation before deciding?

hero.title: A Thoughtful Next Step in Your Fertility Journey.
hero.description: Frozen embryo transfer allows embryos frozen in an earlier IVF or ICSI cycle to be thawed and transferred at a later time. We help you plan the cycle that may suit you best.

overview.title: What Is Frozen Embryo Transfer?
paragraphs: Frozen embryo transfer (FET) is a treatment cycle in which an embryo frozen during a previous IVF or ICSI cycle is thawed and transferred to the uterus.
Before transfer, the lining of the uterus is prepared — either in a natural cycle or with medicines — so the transfer can be timed carefully.
overview.note: Whether a natural or medicated cycle is used depends on your history and your specialist's assessment.

faqTitle: Questions You May Have About FET

faqs.question: What is frozen embryo transfer?
faqs.answer: It is a cycle in which an embryo frozen during a previous IVF or ICSI cycle is thawed and transferred to the uterus.

faqs.question: Do I need another egg retrieval?
faqs.answer: Not if suitable embryos are already stored. FET uses embryos frozen in an earlier cycle.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a natural and a medicated cycle?
faqs.answer: In a natural cycle, transfer is timed with your own ovulation. In a medicated cycle, hormone medicines prepare the uterine lining. Your specialist will advise which may suit you.

faqs.question: Does every embryo survive thawing?
faqs.answer: Not always. Many embryos survive thawing, but some may not. Your team will update you on the day of transfer.

faqs.question: Is embryo transfer painful?
faqs.answer: Experiences vary. Embryo transfer is usually a short procedure, and many people describe it as similar to a routine pelvic examination.

faqs.question: How can I understand the cost of FET?
faqs.answer: Costs depend on the cycle type, medicines and procedures. The clearest way to understand the cost for your situation is to speak with our team.

faqs.question: Can I book a consultation before deciding?
faqs.answer: Yes. A consultation is a chance to review your stored embryos, discuss timing and ask questions.
